input: Research Boeing (boeing.com) for a hedge fund

results_vs_guidance.claim: Q3 ended 2026-09-30: revenue was $24.188 billion, up 4% year over year; GAAP loss per share was $0.26, core loss per share was $0.34, and free cash flow was positive $464 million.
Q3 core loss of $0.34 per share was worse than the $0.21 loss expected by LSEG consensus.
Boeing retained its $2 billion FY2026 free-cash-flow expectation despite negative $359 million through 2026-09-30, but said it would miss its 2026 target of 500 737 deliveries.

Reuters, citing Jefferies, reported expected 2027 free cash flow of $3 billion versus $5.5 billion consensus. Boeing's $10 billion annual free-cash-flow target was placed in 2029, one year later than investor consensus.

credit_signals.claim: Quarter-end liquidity comprised $20.7 billion of cash and marketable investments plus $10.0 billion of undrawn credit facilities, against $45.9 billion of consolidated debt.
The Q3 filing disclosed a $3 billion, 364-day revolving credit agreement entered into in August 2026 and expiring in August 2027.
The Q3 filing reported compliance with all debt and credit-facility covenants and investment-grade ratings: Fitch BBB-/Positive, S&P BBB-/Stable and Moody's Baa3/Stable.

missing_fields: catalysts.confirmed_next_earnings_date: not verified on the opened company calendar.
output.research_view: As of 2026-11-10, Boeing is an execution-led recovery: the key question is whether certified products and firm orders translate into deliveries and cash. The delayed production ramp, newly planned workforce cuts and weaker forward cash-flow outlook make operating evidence more important than headline order growth. My near-term focus would be monthly deliveries and stabilization of the 737 line, with supplier disruption and fixed-price defense losses the principal downside checks.

event_driven.claim: The Q3 filing disclosed an August 9 agreement to sell Insitu, Wisk Aero and SkyGrid to Archer. Consideration includes Archer shares equal to 19.75% of its pre-closing Class A shares and two warrants to purchase up to $200 million of additional stock; closing remained conditional and was expected later in 2026.

Boeing made no open-market common-stock purchases under a repurchase program during Q3. The 25,949 shares received from employees were for tax withholding on restricted-stock vesting, not discretionary buybacks.

catalysts.date: Late 2026 — expected, not a firm closing date
catalysts.claim: Potential completion of the Archer asset sale is a near-term portfolio catalyst. Boeing's October 27 filing expected closing later in 2026, subject to regulatory approval and customary conditions; a completed closing was not verified.

As reported October 27, Boeing targeted stabilization at 47 737s per month in early 2027, versus earlier expectations of reaching that pace in summer 2026. Evidence of achieving—or missing—this milestone is the key operating catalyst.

A new FAA directive for certain 787-8/-9/-10 aircraft becomes effective, requiring radio-altimeter coaxial-cable replacement. The November 9 rule allows a five-year compliance period, so the effective date should not be confused with an immediate fleet-wide repair deadline.

risks.claim: Production recovery remains the central cash-flow risk: the Q3 filing explicitly says delays in future production-rate increases are already adversely affecting financial position, operating results and cash flow.

Fixed-price defense exposure persists: Boeing increased the VC-25B reach-forward loss by $312 million during the first nine months of 2026. KC-46A supplier shortages caused significant Q3 factory disruption and abnormal costs; the filing warns of possible additional losses on both programs.

Safety remediation remains an execution risk: the FAA's new 787 directive addresses unreliable radio-altimeter outputs that could compromise continued safe flight and landing. It covers an estimated 169 U.S.-registered aircraft; the rule's cost estimates concern operators, not a confirmed Boeing charge.

alternative_signals.claim: Boeing announced plans to reduce its commercial-airplane workforce by about 5% through layoffs and attrition, with notifications beginning in December. Management attributed overstaffing to slower production growth; these are planned reductions, not completed layoffs.
October channel check: Bloomberg, citing Cirium data and Jefferies, estimated about 32 737 MAX deliveries versus 43 in September. This was an estimate, not an official Boeing monthly delivery count.
Avolon finalized a firm order for 140 737-10 aircraft, taking its unfilled 737 MAX orders above 240—a demand counterweight to Boeing's production problems.

Leeham reported that Vaero's wing-component supply interruption stalled Everett wing production for several weeks. Shipments had resumed, but Boeing's CFO said the production gap and related abnormal expenses would flow through subsequent quarters.
Boeing received a seven-year contract framework intended to triple PAC-3 MSE seeker production, supporting the defense demand pipeline.
The U.S. Navy selected Boeing to design, build and deliver the F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter, a significant defense franchise win.

insider_and_ownership.claim: A Form 4 signed November 3 reports director Mortimer J. Buckley's October 30 purchase of 5,820 shares at $171.55 each. His direct holdings after the transaction were 10,250 shares.

Vanguard Capital Management's Schedule 13G, signed April 29, reported 58,558,920 shares, or 7.45%, as of March 31. It certified ordinary-course, non-control ownership; this is historical ownership, not a verified current stake or activist position.

MarketBeat reported that Allen Investment Management reduced its Boeing holding by 9.5% during Q3 2026, selling 89,306 shares and ending with 847,130. This is a lagged quarterly position report, not evidence of November selling.

citations.title: THE BOEING COMPANY — FORM 10-Q, quarterly period ended September 30, 2026
excerpts: **VC-25B Presidential Aircraft** The Company’s firm fixed-price contract for the Engineering and Manufacturing Development (EMD) effort on the U.S. Air Force's (USAF) VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, commonly known as Air Force One, is a $4 billion program to develop and modify two 747-8 commercial aircraft. Contract terms to reset the schedule and adjust the requirements were executed on October 16, 2026, which aligned to the 2025 memorandum of agreement. During 2025, we increased the reach-forward loss on the contract by $60. The increased reach-forward loss in 2025 was due to increases in supplier costs. During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we increased the reach-forward loss by $312 due to higher estimated costs required to complete structural and wiring installation and to satisfy air worthiness certification requirements. Risk remains that we may record additional losses in future periods.

**KC-46A Tanker** In 2011, we were awarded a contract from the USAF to design, develop, manufacture, and deliver four next-generation aerial refueling tankers as well as priced options for 13 annual production lots totaling 179 aircraft. Since 2016, the USAF has authorized 12 low-rate initial production (LRIP) lots for a total of 169 aircraft. The EMD contract and authorized LRIP lots total approximately $33 billion as of September 30, 2026. The KC-46A Tanker is a derivative of the 767 commercial airplane program with the majority of the manufacturing costs being incurred in the 767 factory and the remaining costs being incurred in the military finishing and delivery centers. During 2025, we increased the reach-forward loss on the KC-46A Tanker program by $714. The additional reach-forward loss during 2025 was primarily driven by higher estimated manufacturing and engineering costs for production support. During the third quarter of 2026, shortages from a key supplier began creating significant factory disruption resulting in abnormal production costs which are expensed as incurred. As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $113 of capitalized precontract costs and $219 of potential termination liabilities to suppliers related to a future production lot. Risk remains that we may record additional losses in future periods.

basis.reasoning: The program notes disclose the VC-25B loss increase, KC-46A disruption and warnings of further losses.

citations.title: Boeing to cut about 5% of its commercial plane workforce | Boeing | The Guardian
excerpts: Boeing will cut about 5% of its commercial plane workforce as it moderates the pace of ramping up jet production, the company said on Monday. The company will eliminate the posts through a mix of layoffs and attrition because of a slower ramp-up to “provide our factories and supply chain partners additional time to achieve stability”, said a message to employees from Boeing commercial chief Stephanie Pope. “Adjusting our production schedules and reducing aircraft output puts us in an overstaffed position,” she added.

“While we have made substantial progress, we have not yet fully recovered,” said Pope, who promised to treat employees with “dignity and respect” as the company moves ahead with layoff notifications beginning in December

basis.reasoning: The report attributes the planned reduction, methods, rationale and notification timing to Boeing management.
